sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A **Bode plot** shows \(|H(j\omega)|\) in decibels and \(\angle H(j\omega)\) in degrees against a logarithmic frequency axis. On these axes each pole and zero becomes a straight-line asymptote, so a whole response can be sketched by adding simple pieces.

A real pole at \(\omega_p\) is flat below \(\omega_p\) and falls at \(-20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) above it. Its phase moves from \(0^\circ\) to \(-90^\circ\), passing \(-45^\circ\) at \(\omega_p\). The true magnitude is 3 dB below the corner there. A real zero mirrors this, rising at \(+20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) with \(+90^\circ\) of phase. A pole at the origin gives a straight \(-20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) line with a constant \(-90^\circ\).

To sketch, start from the low-frequency gain, and change the slope by \(\pm20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) at every corner. A complex pair adds \(-40\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) and may show a resonant peak if lightly damped.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Sketch \(H(s) = 40/((1 + s/3)(1 + s/300))\). The low-frequency gain is 32 dB. It falls at \(-20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) from 3 rad/s and at \(-40\) from 300 rad/s. At 30 rad/s the asymptote is 12 dB, the true value about 12 dB, and the phase is about \(-90^\circ\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Forgetting that the true curve is 3 dB below the asymptote at a corner.
- Starting the phase change at the corner instead of a decade below.
- Using \(10\log\) for magnitude.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Bode plots of the loop gain give the gain and phase margins used to judge closed-loop stability.
